title: Useful farsi phrases for americans traveling to the middle east
summary: This is a short humorous mock phrasebook, a satirical parody of the pocket guides travellers buy before a trip. Its entries pair a pseudo-Farsi phrase, written in a deliberately garbled transliteration, with an English rendering that is absurd, menacing, or grotesquely polite. Rather than teaching anything useful, the jokes turn the conventions of the genre inside out: a traveller thanks a host for showing off a gun, agrees to lie face down on the floor, accepts a ride in the boot of a car, or offers to betray his country and name American spies in exchange for mercy. Other lines are mock-courtly or bizarre, such as praising water-soaked bread crumbs or preferring a hostage's fate to a fortnight with a celebrity. The humour relies on the gap between polite tourist speech and the hostile, unpredictable situations that a Western visitor might imagine facing abroad. The text is a single short piece of comic writing, so its wider scope is limited to these brief, punchline-driven exchanges.
